old_title: Orbit for Mac in 2026: What It Does, What It Costs, Who It Fits
old_content:
What Happens When You Trap All Your Google Stuff in One Window?

Orbit for Mac does something pretty straightforward: it lets you access every Google account you own from a single window. No more switching between browsers, logging out and in, or managing a million tabs. Just one clean interface that holds Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Google Photos, and everything else Google-related all in one place.

I know what you're thinking. Why does this matter? For freelancers juggling multiple clients, multiple Google accounts, and multiple projects, it actually matters a lot.

Why Would a Freelancer Even Need This?

Let me paint the picture. Marcus, a web designer I know, was managing six different Google accounts. One for his agency work, one for his personal brand, one for each of three clients he consulted with, and one for his side project. Every single day he'd be switching between browser windows, losing track of emails, missing calendar invites because they were in the wrong account window, and spending maybe 15 minutes just navigating between them.

That's where Orbit comes in.

Instead of six browser windows or constantly logging in and out, Marcus now opens Orbit once and has access to all six accounts simultaneously. His Gmail inboxes sit side by side. His calendars are visible at the same time. He can drag files between accounts without any weird export-import nonsense. For someone billing hourly, those 15 minutes add up fast.

Does the Interface Actually Feel Clean, or Is It Just Cramped?

I was worried Orbit would feel like staring at a wall of information. Instead, it's surprisingly organized. The left sidebar lets you switch between your different Google accounts with one click. The main panel shows whatever you're looking at from whichever account you selected. It doesn't try to do anything fancy or confusing.

The design is minimal.

There are no unnecessary animations, no weird color schemes, no trying to be trendy. It's just functional. You open it, click the account you want, and get to work. That simplicity is honestly refreshing compared to tools that try to do everything under the sun.

What About Managing Multiple Accounts at the Same Time?

This is where things get interesting. You can split the window and view two accounts side by side if you're on a larger monitor. So Marcus could have his agency Gmail on the left and a client's Google Drive on the right. He can compare documents, check emails from different perspectives, and move between contexts without losing his place.

But here's the catch: it's not like a proper split-screen workspace builder. You can't have Gmail from one account and Calendar from another account both visible simultaneously. It's account-based splitting, not feature-based. If you need to glance at your personal calendar while responding to a client email from another account, you'll still need to switch tabs.

That limitation annoyed me when I first tested it.

Is the Free Plan Actually Usable, or Is It Just a Demo?

Orbit offers a free version that lets you add multiple accounts and access all the basic switching features. No time limits, no feature restrictions, just genuinely free. You're not getting upsold every five seconds or watching a countdown timer before the app stops working.

The paid version adds some extras like keyboard shortcuts for faster switching and some organizational features, but honestly? Most freelancers I know are fine with the free tier. It does the one thing it's supposed to do, and it does it without asking for your credit card.

What Actually Broke or Frustrated Me?

When I first set up Orbit with my test accounts, I added seven different Google accounts. The app loaded them all fine, but then I realized I'd accidentally added one account twice. I couldn't figure out how to remove duplicates from the interface. I had to dig through the settings menu for a solid ten minutes before finding the option to manage accounts. It should've been more obvious.

Also, Orbit is Mac only. If you're a freelancer who bounces between a Mac at home and a Windows machine at a coffee shop, this won't help you on the Windows side. That's not a flaw with the app itself, but it's worth knowing upfront.

One more thing: notifications can get overwhelming if you have multiple accounts with heavy email traffic. Orbit will ping you for every incoming email across all accounts, and there's no built-in way to prioritize which account's notifications matter most. You end up muting notifications entirely or dealing with constant pings.

How Does It Compare to Just Using Chrome Profiles?

Feature Orbit for Mac Chrome Profiles
Multiple Google accounts visible at once Yes (split view) No (one profile at a time)
Dedicated Mac app Yes No (browser dependent)
Switching speed One click Multiple clicks
Cost Free or paid Free
Cross-account drag and drop Yes Limited
Memory usage Lighter Heavier (multiple Chrome instances)

Would I Actually Use This Full Time?

Yeah, I would. The friction it removes is real. I'm not spending my day wrestling with browser tabs, clearing cookies, or managing separate windows. It's just there, and it works.

But it's not magic. It's a tool that solves one specific problem for people with one specific problem. If you only have one Google account, or if you're happy with your current setup, Orbit won't revolutionize anything for you. If you're juggling multiple accounts and losing time switching between them, it'll save you hours every month.

For freelancers especially, time saved is money earned. Orbit doesn't waste your time, and that's kind of the whole point.

Should You Actually Pay For This?

The free version is genuinely functional. But if you're a freelancer billing clients, the paid tier's keyboard shortcuts and advanced account management might be worth the cost. Quick switching means less mental overhead, and less mental overhead means you stay focused on actual work.

It's not expensive either way.

The question isn't whether you can afford it. The question is whether you're losing enough time with your current setup to justify downloading a new app. If you manage three or more Google accounts regularly, the answer is probably yes.

Does It Actually Integrate With Other Tools?

Orbit is intentionally simple. It doesn't try to integrate with Zapier, Asana, or any of the other productivity tools you might use. It's a window into Google's ecosystem, not a bridge between ecosystems.

That's actually fine. Most freelancers use Google Workspace or regular Gmail anyway. Orbit just makes that better. If you need it to talk to other apps, you're looking at the wrong tool.

My Final Take

Orbit for Mac is boring in the best way possible. It doesn't try to be everything. It just solves one problem cleanly, and it does that without getting in your way. For freelancers managing multiple Google accounts, it saves time and reduces frustration. The free version is legitimately useful, and the paid tier offers extras if you want them. It won't change your life, but it'll make your day a little less annoying.
